name: Millhaven
region: Lordaeron, first village of any size below the hills where the road from the Pass meets the farm roads

sensoryProfile.sight: A long shallow fold of land where two roads cross (theirs from the north, another east-west); a stream along the bottom under a stone bridge; a mill by the bridge with its wheel still, the water still pouring down the race, white even in the dark; an inn with a yard, outside stair, gallery and hanging sign at the crossing; a few dozen low thatched houses with gardens behind them and lanes between garden walls; no smoke, no lit windows. Chapter 3 adds: cobbled crossing with a well at its dead middle and four roads running away from it; a wheelwright's open-fronted shop with a half-built wheel; a smithy; a handcart; coats on every peg; a big brindled barn cat; the great mill wheel standing still, dripping, green weed furring the paddles.
sensoryProfile.sound: Water over the race, the same pitch hour after hour, loud in the night; the inn sign creaking on its bracket ('a dry complaint and a pause and the same complaint again'); the inn door knocking against its frame in the east wind; hooves ringing on the cobbles and running ahead between the houses; the windlass of the well squealing; no dogs, no voices, no work sounds. At night 'it was loud' with silence.
sensoryProfile.smell: Cold hearth-ash and wet thatch, sour milk gone off in a crock from one kitchen, 'no rot under it'. Inn cellar: spilled beer gone sour, apples going soft in straw. Storehouse: pale grain dust. End-house cellar: cold earth, damp, piss and turnips. Taproom at dawn: cold ash, old beer, lantern tallow.
sensoryProfile.touch: Cold stone; cobbles wet; the well rope damp all the way up and 'slick with green'; the staff buzzing in the hand; frost on the cobbles round the mage's hand. The wrongness is 'knotted in one hard lump under the crossroads' (Ch2). Elves cannot feel it directly (Ch3).
sensoryProfile.atmosphere: A village that stopped mid-routine; no panic, no violence, no bodies; every door shut or open as its owners left it; at night 'the first dead village she had sat in through the dark and listened to'.

establishedFacts.fact: Jaina saw Millhaven's name on her road maps coming north: the first village of any size below the hills.
It is where every ruled line on Jaina's map converges ('Most of them cross within a mile of the Millhaven crossroads. The rest miss it by less than the width of your pen').
From the crest, no smoke from any chimney, no lights in windows, no dogs.

The leylines come in from the north, east and west to the crossing 'like the running rigging on her father's flagship coming in through its blocks'; the contamination lies along them and is a hard knot at the crossing.

Millhaven is entirely dead of living people except one cellar-hidden girl (found chapter 3). No bodies and no blood anywhere; no broken doors; coats on pegs; no dogs and no chains; one barn cat, plainly healthy and unbothered.

Layout (from the walk-in and sweep): the crossing has a well at its dead middle and four roads leading away: north (up which the party came), east road, west road, south road. The stream runs below a stone bridge; the mill and a stone storehouse stand on the near side of the bridge; the inn stands at the crossing with a yard, wall, outside stair and gallery above the door; the smithy is on the east side. A wheelwright's shop is the first building past the inn on the west side. A lane runs behind the east-side gardens between the garden walls and the first field; it is churned to ridges and holes a boot deep. A five-barred oak field gate at the top of the lane (open, rope loop over the post) leads to the drove way (the cow way).

Timing of the stop: Cyndia's read of the east side is 'I'd say they went a few at a time'. Sylvanas's inference from the grey fur on the bowls in the end house: 'Five days at the most.' The wheelwright laid down his drawknife 'in the middle of the day with the light still good'. Houses show people stopped at different hours (breakfast, supper, a sickbed).
Millhaven has had a market day (per the old carter, who says he was 'through here on market day' and they were 'well enough then'; unreconciled with 'five days').
The inn door has a horseshoe nailed over the lintel with the points down (a human way of letting the luck pour out over whoever walks in).
A wooden horse with a short leg lies under the table of the last house on the west side; Sylvanas moved it onto the table.
The girl calls the way the dead went 'the north road'; it is the drove way past Pell's, running north and a little east, not the Pass road.

charactersPresentHere: the old carter (briefly, at the bridge and crossing)

eventsHere.event: Party halts on the crest above the village at dusk and walks down in formation, bows in hand, at the end of chapter 2.

The party rides in at last light; the horses spook; Sylvanas orders a perimeter, a sweep in pairs and horses to the inn yard; houses swept, nothing found; the well read; the mage goes under and is pulled out; the inn cellar and storehouse read; the lane behind the east gardens is found churned; the end-house hatch is found and the girl is brought out; the party holds the village overnight (inn gallery watch).

At first light the party reads the drove way (sixty at least), writes the dispatch, sends Neral, the girl and the fourth ranger north, meets the old carter at the bridge and leaves south across the bridge.
